newsitem.title: GERMANY: Book by spymaster Wolf slammed by German leaders.
newsitem.headline: Book by spymaster Wolf slammed by German leaders.

text.p: Markus Wolf, the legendary East German spymaster, was accused by leading German politicians on Wednesday of greed and slander for his forthcoming book that lifts the lid on a number of embarrassing Cold War secrets.

Wolf's book -- which says the CIA offered him a house, a small fortune, and a new identity in California in exchange for secrets -- will be distributed on June 2 in 14 countries and 11 languages. Excerpts will be published in Stern magazine on Thursday.

Wolfgang Thierse, an eastern German leader of the opposition Social Democrats, said the charges by Wolf that the powerful post-war West German SPD parliamentary leader Wolfgang Wehner was an East German spy was a cheap marketing ploy.
"This is unsubstantiated slander he is using to sell books," Thierse said. "It leaves a bitter taste in my mouth to see the criminals twisting history to fit their version of events."
The book "Markus Wolf -- Spy Chief in a Secret War", says the CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence agency both tried to recruit Wolf shortly after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
The story begins like a spy novel, with a recently retired CIA officer named Gardner Hathaway visiting Wolf's home outside Berlin in May 1990.
Wolf says Hathaway brought chocolates and flowers and began by heaping praise on Wolf's spectacular 30-year career leading one of the world's most successful spy agencies.

Hathaway told Wolf he had come on behalf of CIA director William Webster, offering to help Wolf escape from German prosecutors preparing charges against him in exchange for Wolf's help in identifying KGB agents operating in the United States.
According to excerpts being published in Stern magazine, the CIA offered a California house, a new identity and more than $100,000 for his help.
"California is a nice place with great weather," Hathaway told Wolf.
"Siberia isn't bad either," Wolf replied, adding he doubted he would be of value because he would never betray the identities of his agents. "The names of my agents are taboo."
Wolf said he also turned down a similar offer from the West German secret service.

"Herr Wolf, just 10 or 12 names and a few details about how the actions of your agency affected security in West Germany and you won't have to worry about prosecution," Wolf quotes former East German interior minister Peter-Michael Diestel as saying.
Wolf writes that West German Interior Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble was behind that offer, which he also turned down.

Wolf was long referred to by Western intelligence as the "Man Without a Face" because they did not know what he looked like. Thriller writers often took him as a model when depicting a sinister communist spy chief.

Wolf ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside then chancellor Willy Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
He was convicted in 1993 of treason but that ruling was overturned by Germany's highest court in 1995.
A verdict in a second trial, where Wolf has been charged with masterminding three Cold War kidnappings, is due on May 27.
